What is bridge i'm assuming its a 2v2 with the 52 card deck?

Yes, the suite of a card is important, highest card of the suite played in a trick(round) wins, if there are no trump cards. A trump card is a particular suite, that wins the round. So for example, if spades are trump cards, a spade 2 beats a club ace. Your partner is the person facing you across the table. No verbal communication between partners is allowed. To begin play, a person is chosen as the declarer, the player to the declarers left plays the opening lead, then the declarers partner displays his hand. this exposed hand is called the dummy, and reveals valuable information, and is really what bridge is all about. Even with one hand exposed, there is plenty of mystery. Bidding is another part of bridge, that really gets into strategy, and knowing your partner, and how they play bridge.

After looking at his cards, each player in turn, beginning with the dealer, must make a call. A call is a pass, bid, double or redouble. A pass means what it sounds like. If all 4 players pass, the round is passed out, and the cards are reshuffled. A bid is a statement to win a specific number of tricks with a specific suit as trumps (or with no suit as trumps). Each bid must state a number from one to seven, which is the number of tricks in addition to six that the bidder agrees to win. Each bid must specify the suit (spades, hearts, diamonds or clubs) that will be trumps or no-trump if the bidder wishes to play without a trump suit. For example, a bid of four spades is a statement to win 10 tricks (six plus four) with spades as the trump suit. A bid of three no-trump is a statement to win nine tricks (six plus three) without a trump suit. Each successive bid around the table must name a higher number than the preceding bid, or name an equal number in a higher ranking suit (or no-trump). You can't bid higher than seven, because that would be stating your intent to win 14 tricks/rounds, when you have only 13 cards! You can double the previous bid, if an opponent made the bid. This is a good move, if you have a strong hand, and you can even double down(redouble) if you're really confident! The final bid becomes the contract. If the contract names a suit, all cards in that suit become trump. So you see, the bidding takes place before the playing of the cards.

So the declarer is whoever first bid the trump suite (or no-trump). The player to the left of the declarer plays the opening lead, and immediately after the opening lead is made, the dummy spreads his entire hand face up, arranged into suits for all to see. The declarer plays both his and the dummy's hands, playing the correct suite when possible. Play 13 tricks, and you've played a game of Bridge! If this seems overwhelming, that's because it is very complicated, and may take a few games to properly understand. I recommend first learning to play Whist, the simpler, original, form of Bridge, as that's how I started out.
